gloss_terse: Daintiness, luxury, exquisite delight; refined pleasure or pampered tenderness
gloss_readable: The Hebrew noun ta'anug conveys a sense of luxurious pleasure, refined delight, and pampered tenderness. In Proverbs 19:10 it describes a lifestyle of luxury ill-suited to a fool, while Ecclesiastes 2:8 uses the plural for Solomon's accumulated delights. In Song of Songs 7:6 it appears in an intimate address to the beloved, linking sensory pleasure with love. Micah 1:16 and 2:9 shift the register toward tender affection—'dainty sons' and 'dainty houses'—things precious that will be lost in judgment.

senses.1: Luxury, refined pleasure, exquisite delight. Covers the full semantic range from material indulgence (Prov 19:10; Eccl 2:8) to tender affection for loved ones (Mic 1:16; 2:9) and the delight of love (Song 7:6). Spanish 'deleite' and 'delicias,' French 'délices,' and English 'delights' all converge on the notion of pleasure that is both sensory and emotionally precious—something savored rather than merely possessed.

gloss_terse: Tappuah; a Canaanite place name meaning 'apple,' designating towns in Judah and Ephraim-Manasseh
gloss_readable: Tappuah ('apple' or 'apple-town') names at least two distinct locations in the promised land. One lies in the lowland of Judah (Josh 15:34), and another sits on the contested border between Ephraim and Manasseh (Josh 12:17; 16:8; 17:8), where the related 'En-Tappuah' ('spring of Tappuah') appears. The Septuagint renders the name variously as Taphouth, Thapphous, and Thapheth, reflecting the difficulty ancient translators had stabilizing this toponym.

senses.1: Tappuah—a proper geographic name for Canaanite towns conquered and allocated to Israel. All five occurrences (Josh 12:17; 15:34; 16:8; 17:8 twice) function as place references. Translations uniformly transliterate: English 'Tappuach,' Spanish 'Tapúa,' French and German 'Tappuach,' confirming this is a stable proper noun requiring no semantic disambiguation.

gloss_terse: Whitewash; a coating of plaster used to cover walls, metaphorically for false assurances
gloss_readable: In Ezekiel's prophetic visions, taphel refers to the whitewash that false prophets smear over a flimsy wall—making it look solid when it is not. The literal image appears in Ezekiel 13:10–15, where God promises rain, hailstones, and wind will expose the shoddy construction. In 22:28, the same term functions as a sharp metaphor: the prophets 'whitewash' their lies, coating falsehood with a veneer of divine authority. German 'Tünche' captures this precisely.

senses.1: Whitewash, plaster coating applied to conceal structural weakness. All five occurrences cluster in Ezekiel (13:10, 11, 14, 15; 22:28), where it serves both as a literal building material and a prophetic metaphor for deceptive reassurance. English 'whitewash,' Spanish 'cal' (lime), and German 'Tünche' all point to a surface treatment that hides what lies beneath—perfectly suited to Ezekiel's indictment of false prophecy.

gloss_terse: Strong, mighty, powerful; used of kingdoms, fearsome beasts, and divine wonders (Aramaic)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic adjective taqqiph describes formidable strength in Daniel and Ezra. In Daniel 2:40 and 2:42, it characterizes the iron-like kingdom in Nebuchadnezzar's dream. Daniel 7:7 applies it to the terrifying fourth beast, while Daniel 4:3 (ET 3:33) ascribes it to God's mighty wonders. Ezra 4:20 notes that Jerusalem once had 'mighty kings' who ruled beyond the river. The word always carries overtones of dominance and awe-inspiring power.

senses.1: Strong, mighty, powerful—describing entities that command fear or awe. Applied to an iron-crushing kingdom (Dan 2:40, 42), a terrifying beast (Dan 7:7), divine signs (Dan 4:3), and historically dominant kings (Ezra 4:20). Spanish distinguishes 'fuerte' (strong) from 'poderosos/poderosas' (powerful/mighty), hinting at the range from raw material strength to political and divine might that this single Aramaic adjective covers.

gloss_terse: To grow strong, become mighty; in Pael, to enforce or make stringent (Aramaic)
gloss_readable: The Aramaic verb teqeph describes the process of becoming powerful or hardened. In Daniel 4, the great tree 'grew strong' (4:11, 20), mirroring Nebuchadnezzar's expanding dominion, and the king himself is told 'you have become strong' (4:22). A darker nuance emerges in 5:20, where hardened arrogance leads to downfall. The Pael stem in 6:7 shifts to causative meaning: 'to enforce' or make an interdict binding. Spanish captures both poles—'se hizo fuerte' (grew strong) and 'para imponer' (to enforce).

senses.1: To grow strong, become mighty, or harden (Pe'al stem). Describes organic or political growth in power, applied to the symbolic tree (Dan 4:11, 20), the king's authority (Dan 4:22), and the dangerous hardening of a proud spirit (Dan 5:20). The Pael infinitive in Dan 6:7 extends the meaning to 'enforce, make stringent'—applying strength to a legal decree. The multilingual evidence shows translations oscillating between natural growth ('became strong') and volitional imposition ('to enforce').

gloss_terse: Deceitfulness, treachery; the quality of deception especially in false prophecy and faithless hearts
gloss_readable: Tarmith denotes a deep-seated deceitfulness—the treachery that lodges in the human heart and on the tongue. Jeremiah uses it to diagnose Israel's spiritual sickness: the people cling to 'perpetual deceit' (8:5) and false prophets speak from 'the deceit of their own heart' (14:14; 23:26). The psalmist in 119:118 dismisses those whose falsehood (sheqer) is itself deceitful (tarmith). Zephaniah 3:13 envisions a purified remnant whose tongue harbors no deceit.

senses.1: Deceitfulness, treachery—a quality of persistent falsehood rooted in the heart or tongue. Appears exclusively in prophetic and wisdom contexts: paired with sheqer ('falsehood') in Ps 119:118 and Jer 23:26, with kazav ('lie') and 'awlah ('injustice') in Zeph 3:13, and describing incorrigible apostasy in Jer 8:5. Spanish 'engaño' and English 'deceit' align closely, while the French rendering 'Tubal' for one occurrence appears to be a textual anomaly, underscoring how this rare noun can confound translators.

gloss_terse: Tirshatha; title of the Persian-appointed governor of Judah, meaning 'His Excellency' or 'the revered one'
gloss_readable: Tirshatha is a Persian loanword used as an honorific title for the governor of post-exilic Judah. It appears in Ezra 2:63 and Nehemiah 7:65 for an unnamed governor who restricts priestly privileges until the Urim and Thummim can be consulted, and in Nehemiah 8:9; 10:1 it explicitly designates Nehemiah himself. The title likely derives from a Persian root meaning 'feared, revered,' functioning much like 'His Excellency' in diplomatic usage.

senses.1: Tirshatha—a Persian-derived gubernatorial title meaning 'the revered one' or 'His Excellency,' applied to the governor of Judah in the post-exilic period. All five occurrences (Ezra 2:63; Neh 7:65, 70; 8:9; 10:1) carry the Hebrew article ha- ('the'), marking it as a recognized official designation. English and Spanish render it as 'the Tirshata'/'the governor' (el gobernador), while French and German transliterate the Hebrew directly, reflecting the foreignness of this Persian administrative term in a Hebrew text.

gloss_terse: Alpha; the first letter of the Greek alphabet, used as a divine title meaning 'the First' or 'the Beginning'
gloss_readable: Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, deployed in Revelation as a majestic self-designation of God and the risen Christ. In the phrase 'I am the Alpha and the Omega,' it declares absolute primacy—the one who stands at the origin of all things. All four occurrences appear in Revelation (1:8, 11; 21:6; 22:13), always paired with Omega to form a merism encompassing all of reality from first to last. Every major translation simply transliterates: Alpha across English, Spanish, French, and German.

senses.1: Alpha as a christological and theological title—the first letter of the Greek alphabet functioning as a divine self-designation meaning 'the First' or 'the Beginning.' Paired with Omega in all four Revelation passages (1:8, 11; 21:6; 22:13), it forms an A-to-Z merism claiming sovereignty over all existence. The universal transliteration across languages (English 'Alpha,' Spanish 'Alfa,' French 'Alpha,' German 'Alpha') reflects its status as an irreducible symbolic name rather than a translatable concept.

gloss_terse: Abel; the second son of Adam, whose righteous offering and innocent blood became a type of faithful martyrdom
gloss_readable: Abel, from Hebrew hevel, names Adam's second son whose sacrifice God accepted and whose murder by Cain became the Bible's first instance of innocent blood shed. In the New Testament, Jesus invokes 'the blood of Abel' (Matt 23:35; Luke 11:51) as the starting point of a long history of righteous bloodshed. Hebrews 11:4 holds Abel up as the first exemplar of faith, and 12:24 contrasts his blood—which cries for justice—with Christ's blood, which speaks a better word.

senses.1: Abel as a proper name designating Adam's righteous second son, functioning in the NT as a typological figure of faithful martyrdom. Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51 cite his blood as the opening chapter of innocent suffering, while Hebrews 11:4 and 12:24 develop his theological significance—faith that speaks even after death. Translations consistently transliterate: English 'Abel'/'Habel,' Spanish 'Hábel,' French 'Abel,' German 'Abel,' preserving the Hebrew name across all traditions.

gloss_terse: Goodness, uprightness, moral excellence; an active benevolence that goes beyond mere kindness
gloss_readable: Agathosyne denotes a robust moral goodness—not passive innocence but an active, generous uprightness that shapes how a person lives and relates to others. Paul lists it among the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22) and as a component of the Spirit's light (Eph 5:9), pairing it with righteousness and truth. In Romans 15:14, he affirms that the Roman believers are 'full of goodness,' and in 2 Thessalonians 1:11, he prays that God would fulfill every desire for goodness. It is virtue with agency.

senses.1: Active moral goodness, generous uprightness—a quality that goes beyond passive decency to express benevolent character in action. All four NT occurrences are Pauline: listed as a fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22), paired with righteousness and truth as the 'fruit of light' (Eph 5:9), affirmed as a quality of mature believers (Rom 15:14), and prayed for as a divine gift (2 Thess 1:11). Spanish 'bondad,' French 'bonté,' German 'Güte,' and English 'goodness' all converge, yet the Pauline contexts push beyond generic niceness toward a Spirit-empowered moral vitality.
